Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <3c0c2432.182656612@news>, Talo...@hotmail.com writes:
>Well sure, but I was mainly thinking of locations. Africa, Russia,
>South America, IndoAsia and the like just aren't represented at all.

Partly, some locations aren't terribly well represented in the WoD.
This is not altogether surprising, for two main reasons IMO.

Firstly, White Wolf will often want to appeal to their player-base in a
manner that will generate sales. Certain areas aren't going to be
terribly interesting for people. Lots of people will buy Washington DC
by Night, or similar, whereas far fewer people would buy, say, Niger by
Night.

Secondly, in purely "practical" terms, there are numerous locations that
would be difficult for Vampire mechanics. For example, vampires living
in very northern Europe (parts of Russia/ex-USSR and Scandinavia) will
have this small problem with daylight for a lot of the year, followed by
no problem at all. Similarly, a vampire living in a particularly
tropical climate will have problems with only having a relatively few
hours of darkness.

Such provides numerous technical, practical difficulties for players to
overcome. If players are spending their time trying to work out how to
cheat a system that's basically designed for temperate climates with
fairly substantial portions of both daylight and darkness on a regular
basis, they're spending a lot less time Storytelling - which is *the*
point of the games White Wolf design.

The scarcity of them in the WoD makes it far harder to convincingly
portray them in V:TES - which is partly being sourced from such.

Also, in the WoD, other factions thrive in other locations. Making
*every* location into a vampire strong-hold makes it difficult to
generate strong games. That the Changing Breeds are adapted to and
strong in certain locations where Kindred aren't makes for a different
environment. Of course, there's plenty of scope for cross-over in some
places, but having each group exist in its own little niche *as well*
provides a number of opportunities that wouldn't be provided otherwise.

(Some parts of Indo-Asia also have some potential for Kindred of the
East, anyway.)

On a separate issue, Russia/ex-USSR is likely to provide a number of
problems of handling it. How involved do you make vampires in the rise
and fall of communism and the Cold War? Such would be, were I a
designer, terribly difficult to decide - can I justify making my
vampires responsible for the killing of 10 million people or more during
World War II and its aftermath? Can I justify the Cold War? Do I want
to end up treading on potentially *extremely* sensitive subjects? How
do I explain Gorbachov's actions? This isn't going to be easy.

Black Dog, however, might provide a possible channel for such, akin to
the Charnel Houses Wraith supplement.

--

Baba Yaga isn't Niktuku. She's the one childe of Absimilliard
(Nosferatu) that wasn't Bound to him, and escaped. The Niktuku have
been hunting her, and her progeny, ever since. All Nosferatu are
descended from her. They fear Baba Yaga because she would rather kill
her own than let them lead the Niktuku to her.

Nights of Prophecy chronicles the fall of Baba Yaga rather well.

As for geographic expansions...

The Children of Caine flourish in Europe and North America. In
Russia, Baba Yaga and Durga Syn were the only vampires of any
respectable power -- most others were silenced by Baba Yaga or the
Shadow Curtain.

Africa and South America, particularly the Amazon Basin, are
strongholds of the shifting breeds, and any vampire there is going to
be short-lived. They made great locations for Rage expansions -- but
it would be inappropriate for a vampire expansion.

legb...@my-deja.com (legbiter) wrote in message news:<68f2e9f8.01112...@posting.google.com>...

> i think Dark Ages is a MUCH better bet for an expansion.

I agree. There's some scope here for a stand-alone game that still
provides value to the existing V:TES card pool too.

Consider the following:
You have crypt cards with different coloured backs (say, purple) to
the orange ones we have at present, these are the Dark Ages (DA)
vampires and can't ever be used with existing crypt cards. The library
cards remain the same however. This allows you to add new library
cards that can be used in the modern game and prevents modern and DA
vampire being played at the same time. So whilst new Protean cards
could be used in the modern game, DA clan specific cards could not
(and to some extent DA clan discipline specific cards too, unless Ian
Forestal wants to do some hard research). You could also have cards
with a 'usable only by a DA vampire' clause if required.

This takes care of unsatisfactory crossovers with DA vampires tooling
up with Assault Rifles (well, in tournaments anyway) and Cappadocians
running around in the modern game. Other advantages include the chance
to reprint cards, have younger versions of modern vampires and run DA
exclusive tournaments that have a limited card pool without totally
disadvantaging the older players who can still use their modern
library cards as long as that card has been reprinted in DA.

All of this would expand the current game and provide a new tournament
format that is more newb friendly and has engineered certain cards and
strategies out of the game to replace them with new ones.

Sound good?

matt.

I've been a CCG playtester for various games. From what I've seen, the
playtesters have to make do as best they can given the time frame predetermined
by the company's need to put out product to make money. How well they do is
likely a function of 1) how well the process is managed and 2) how many
playtesters there are. Magic may be the only CCG that gets sufficient
playtesting and mistakes are still made.

The role of the typical CCG playtester, which probably doesn't include whoever
works on Magic, AFAICT, is horribly overrated by those who've never done it.
You are right about something. When you introduce new playtesters for a set,
usually the time frame is such that they aren't familiar and have no time to
get familiar with the previous set. So, the older playtesters have to deal
with the previous set while the new playtesters muddle through.

As for maintaining balance, what companies have done in the past is weaken the
set to make sure it isn't broken. Usually, longer playtest windows result in
stronger sets as the fear of overpowered cards diminishes and the playtesters
find time to get around to the coasters instead of just being worried about the
broken cards. Good example was Homelands v. Alliances. I specifically recall
reading about how they were too conservative with Homelands due to insufficient
playtesting. But, the answer to that isn't to delay putting out expansions but
to add more playtesters, start the process sooner, and/or better manage the
process.

That's why I prefaced it sales going reasonably well. I'm no expert (
althogh I am an experienced customer :) but I would imagine that most
customers go through three stages of card purchasing.

1) Inital release splurge.
2) Interest is maintained and cards are being bought regularly.
3) Interest wanes and money starts going into other things.

The best way to tell what stage the average customer is in is through sales.
If the product is selling well then Mr Joe average is still in stage 2. It
would be crazy to release a new set because Mr Average won't be spending any
more money and now he's going to have to split it between two different
products. You might get a very minior boost in profits but at the expense of
shortening the overall lifespan if your product.

There is obviously a need for there to be a timeline for expansions so that
the company can plan ahead further enough but I think it's wise to hold off
releasing new sets until demand for existing sets wanes or players are
demanding it even while sales are strong.
